_comment: C0 body translation · gitguardian (2026-11-06). Key contract per cursor.en.json; sources/related counts must match the source file.

axes.model_access: It neither guards a model nor offers model tiers: its main axis is credentials (secrets) and identity. Its relation to models under test has only two surfaces on record — the docs navigation lists a "GitGuardian MCP Server", whose page describes bringing secret security into your AI coding assistant, and ggshield, which covers the IDE and pre-commit/pre-push places "wherever code is written". Swappable detection models: not applicable, since it does pattern matching plus validity checks rather than model evaluation.
axes.runtime: The browser platform is the main interaction surface (the docs navigation covers Platform / Secrets Detection / Internal Monitoring / Public Monitoring / NHI Governance / Endpoint Protection / Honeytoken, and the login entry points at dashboard.gitguardian.com), with scanning and orchestration on the SaaS side. Two local surfaces also exist: ggshield — "Scans run locally" per the docs — and Self-Hosting, worded "set up and run the GitGuardian platform on your infrastructure", which explicitly lists air-gapped environments and two Kubernetes install shapes.
axes.local_files: ggshield scans repositories, directories and diffs on your machine, with documented output formats (json / gitlab / sarif) and commands secret scan, diagnose and ignore-display; the platform side connects your repositories, CI/CD, container registries and collaboration tools (internal monitoring docs: "code repositories to container registries and collaboration tools"). **How long scanned code content is retained vendor-side**: not addressed clause by clause in the public terms, moved to unknowns.
axes.background: Background work is one of its strengths, but ownership differs: the platform monitors continuously (public GitHub monitoring plus the incident lifecycle), while the local side is the instant pre-commit/pre-push interception. SaaS change cadence can be re-read day by day in the docs' SaaS Releases (latest on record the same day: the 2026-10-29 team-sync entry).
axes.tools: The integration surface is systematic in the docs navigation: GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket / Azure, CI (Azure Pipelines, Jenkins), Jira / Slack / Confluence, container registries (including a Harbor entry), Endpoint Protection, Honeytoken (decoy credentials), ggscout and the GitGuardian API. **The MCP surface is on record officially**: the MCP Server page states "Bring secrets security directly into your AI coding assistant" and lists three security constraints — "read-only permissions, server-side scanning, and secret redaction".
axes.context: Its "memory" is an asset and incident ledger, not conversation context: NHI Governance (non-human identity), the incident lifecycle and the monitored perimeter persist inside the platform. Cross-session memory and context windows are not applicable — it generates nothing. Detector history and versions have a separate Detection Engine Releases page (on record in the navigation, not read item by item in this pass).
axes.permissions: Clause by clause with sources: the readable entry for account and data terms is the privacy policy on the site, where the retention sentence reads "Data collected when you request information or when you contact us is kept for two (2) years from our last contact.", and the transfer sentence reads "We may share your Personal Data with our US office, which is located outside of the EEA, in the US."; **whether customer code or matched content is used for training** is not mentioned, and the policy does not state the storage scope of customer code — both go to unknowns. Detection semantics are on record in the engine FAQ: three stages "Pre-Validation", "Matching", "Post-Validation", plus "GitGuardian will check the validity of the detected credentials". Red line: the vendor's "600+ types of hardcoded secrets" is a **count of secret types**; this site never converts it into a blocking or coverage rate and never ranks it against PII tooling — the "Secrets never leave your perimeter" phrasing is only read in the self-hosted/perimeter context.
axes.fit: Fits: credentials and non-human identities already at scale (many repositories plus CI plus containers plus collaboration tools plus AI coding assistants), where the need is continuous monitoring with an incident loop rather than one scan; needing instant interception at pre-commit/pre-push and in the IDE; and when the network-boundary requirement is high, self-hosting or even air-gapped is available. Not a fit: when the constraint is "PII operators must run on my own machine before data reaches a model" (that is the Presidio constraint); when you only want a one-off red-team scan for evidence; or when a secret scanner is expected to replace model evaluation.

runs:
**This site has not run it end to end**: no repository or CI connected, no incident triggered, no ggshield scan executed, so no detection ratio, false-positive rate or ranking is produced. This archive only organises statements on record at the site, the docs navigation, four docs section pages, the engine FAQ, SaaS Releases, the privacy policy and the pricing page.

**Suggested measurements** (four):

- **How validity checking actually behaves** (the FAQ states it happens; the exact call pattern and failure modes are not on record)
- **The feature delta under self-hosted and air-gapped installs** (which integrations and Honeytoken still work offline)
- **How the MCP Server's read-only constraint lands inside a real agent** (the three constraints are on record; the permission model was not verified item by item)
- **Retention of scanned code fragments vendor-side** (not addressed clause by clause; a due-diligence must-ask)
unknowns:
- The certificates and audit artefacts themselves (SOC 2 / ISO 27001 reports, DPA, subprocessor list): /trust and /security returned 404 that day, not disclosed on public pages
- Storage scope and retention period for customer code and matched fragments vendor-side
- Whether customer data trains models (the privacy policy does not mention it)
- Item-by-item contents of Detection Engine Releases and Self-Hosted Releases
- Honeytoken types and the detection chain behind them (listed in navigation, page bodies unread)
- Whether the data-residency region is selectable (the policy only states transfers to the US office)
- The MCP Server permission model and tool inventory
- Mainland-network direct reachability and filing status (not measured, not searched)
related: Both hosted platforms but with different objects: that archive covers PII/source code and agent data movement, this one covers credentials and the incident loop.
Opposite constraint: that archive's operators must run inside your boundary, whereas this one scans vendor-side by default with a self-hosted alternative.
Same red-team line: PyRIT produces records too, and those logs must not carry live credentials either.
